TRIBE TROPIDEAE DRESSLER
1. Corymborkis Thou.
Terrestrial plants with short, sympodial, creeping
rhizomes; roots fasciculate, wiry. Stems erect, terete,
unbranched, leafy, bamboo-like. Leaves plicate, dis-
tichous or spirally arranged, sessile. Inflorescences
axillary, paniculate, few- to many-flowered. Flowers
distichously arranged, often not opening widely,
white, pale green or yellow, fragrant; pedicel short,
twisted. Sepals and petals subsimilar, narrow, basally
connivent. Lip spathulate, with 2 longitudinal keels
embracing the column below. Column elongate, slen-
der; rostellum erect, bifid; pollinia 2.
A pantropical genus of about five species. One is
known from Belize.
ETYMoLoGY. From the Greek corymbos (a cor-
ymb) and orchis (orchid), referring to the inflores-
cence of the type species, C. corymbis Thou.
Corymborkis forcipigera (Rchb. f.) LO. Williams.
in Bot. Mus. Leafi. Harvard Univ. 12: 237 (1946).
Type: Granada, Warscewicz (holo. W!).
Macrostylis forcipigera Rchb. f. in Bonplandia 2: 96
Corymborchis cubensis Acuña in Bol. Téc. 60, Est.
Exp. Agron. Santiago de Las Vagas: 51 (1939).
Plant terrestrial, tall, stout, erect, up to 2 m tall. Stem
terete. Leaves large, crowded on the upper part of
stem, elliptic-lanceolate, distichous, sessile, many-
nerved, up to 45 cm long and 7.5 cm wide. Inflores-
cences 1 to 3, lax, corymbose, paniculate, axillary, up
to 12 cm long. Flowers greenish-white, arcuate;
floral bracts lanceolate, acute, clasping the base.
Sepals canaliculate, fleshy; dorsal sepal linear, in-
curved, up to 19mm long and 2.5 mm wide; lateral
sepals linear-oblanceolate, acute, up to 15 mm long
and 2.5mm wide. Petals oblanceolate, thinner than
sepals, up to 13 mm long and 3.5 mm wide. Lip
arcuate-decurved, spatulate, canaliculate below with
2 longitudinal keels within, up to 14 mm long. Col-
umn arching, apex bluntly acute, reflexed, up to 12
mm long.
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. The West Indies, Me-
xico, Belize, Guatemala and Costa Rica.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Toledo District. Rare.
HABITAT. In rich soil and humus, in forest and
thickets.
FLOWERING SEASON. July.
ETYmoLoGY. From the Latin forcipis (a pair of
tongs, a forceps) and gero (to bear) in allusion to the
flower shape.

2. Erythrodes BI.
Plants terrestrial or semi-epiphytic, small, arising
from a creeping rhizome. Stems erect, sheathed by
bracts or the bases of petiolate leaves. Leaves cauline,
with distinct petioles which are expanded into an
infundibuliform sheath. Inflorescence a terminal ra-

and subtropics of the Americas, Asia, Malaysia and
Oceanic Islands. One is known from Belize.
ETYMOLOGY. From the Greek erythros (red) and
eidos (appearance) referring to the flower colour of
the type species, E latifolia BI.
Erythrodes purpurea (Ames) Ames, Orchid. 5: 28
(1915). Type: Guatemala, Alta Verapaz, H. von

Physurus purpureus Ames, Orchid. 2: 259 (1908).
P. luniferus Schltr. in Fedde, Repert. Sp. Nov. 15: 199
P. argyrostictus Schltr. in Fedde, Repert. Sp. Nov. 16:
Erythrodes lunifera Ames, Orchid. 7: 71 (1922).
Plant terrestrial, erect, slender, up to 30 cm tall. Scape
leafy, pubescent above. Leaves shortly petiolate,
ovate-lanceolate, acute, dark to pale green flecked
with white, abaxially purple to light green, up to 9 cm
long and 3.3 cm wide. Inflorescence racemose,
loosely-flowered; bracts linear-lanceolate, scarious.
Flowers white or greenish-white. Sepals somewhat
pubescent; dorsal sepal linear, up to 5 mm long and
1.8 mm wide; lateral sepals lanceolate, up to 5.5 mm
long and 1.8 mm wide. Petals linear-oblanceolate, up
to 5 mm long and 1.5 mm wide. Lip up to 8.5 mm
long including saccate spur, lateral lobes recurved
and minutely ciliate. (Fig. 1).
GENERAL DISTRIBUTION. Mexico to Honduras,
and Costa Rica.
DISTRIBUTION IN BELIZE. Exact locality not
known. Rare.
HABITAT. In leaf mold or rich soil of wet dense
forest.
FLOWERING SEASON. June and July.
ETYMoLoGY. From the Latin purpureus (purple)
in reference to the original collector's note describing
the leaves as 'dark red violet'
by us.

3 Goodyera
3. Goodyera R. Br.
Small to medium-sized terrestrial plants with a creep-
ing rhizome, rooting at the nodes producing erect
secondary stems. Leaves basal, clustered in lower
part of stem, fleshy, several, petiolate from inflated
sheaths. Inflorescences erect, few- to many-flowered,
racemose; peduncle and rachis pubescent. Flowers
small to insignificant, often pubescent. Sepals paral-
lel to floral axis or with lateral sepals spreading;
dorsal sepal forming a hood with the petals. Lip
hollow or saccate with bristly hairs within. Column
short; rostellum long, deeply cleft; stigma nor divid-
ed; pollinia 2.
A genus of about 40 species, widely distributed in
the northern temperate zone, south to Central Ameri-
ca, S. E. Asia, the Pacific islands and Australia. One is
known from Belize.
ETymoLoGY. Named after John Goodyer (1592-
1664), an early English botanist.
Goodyera erosa (Ames & C. Schweinf.) Ames, E.T.
Hubbard & C. Schweinf. in Bot. Mus. Leafl. Harvard
Univ. 3: 37 (1934). Type: Costa Rica, A.M. Brems 100
(holo. AMES).
Epipactis erosa Ames & C. Schweinf. in Ames,
Sched. Orchid. 10: 9(1930).
Plant terrestrial, up to 40 cm tall. Rhizome decum-
bent, stem-like. Stem short, up to 5 cm tall, enveloped
by loose, imbricating bases of dilated petioles. Lea-
ves up to 4, crowded, petioled, ovate-lanceolate, up to
7 cm long and and 2.4 cm wide. Inflorescence ra-
cemose, up to 11 cm long; floral bracts triangular-
lanceolate. Flowers very small. Sepals sparsely pu-
bescent; lateral sepals triangular-lanceolate, up to 5
mm long and 2 mm wide; dorsal sepal lanceolate, up
to 5 mm long and 2 mm wide. Petals strongly adhe-
rent to the dorsal sepal, up to 5mm long and 2.5 mm
wide. Lip saccate, sides adherent to the column as far
as the clinandrium, up to 5 mm long. Column min
ute.
